title: How minstrel shows worked; Sophie Tucker selling her book
summary: Tent minstrel shows ran full performances with 10-12 acts and sold photographs; he compares it to Sophie Tucker selling books in Miami in 1956.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: About the Minstrel shows, what were they like? What happened?

Well, Minstrel shows were one big tent. They were tent shows -- tent minstrel shows, and there was a large tent, like, not as big as the Big Top with the circus, you know, but it was a big tent, and I think it would seat, like, 3 or 400 people, and that's a lot.

But what you would do if you played county fairs or something, you would do like, 4 or 5 shows a day -- or 5, 6 shows a day, you know, however many people were on the midway, and if the midway was really crowded, now they may not get but a 15 minute show, you know, and they may get more, but that's with the carnival -- but you're asking about the minstrel show?

Now the minstrel show was a full performance at all times, and that was where -- and it seems to me that Ida Cox or somebody was on a minstrel show that we were on -- and they used to; it seems to me we played Baltimore, Maryland. I don't know why -- well, I know why that sticks in my mind, because, you know, as a kid certain things stick out in your mind, and Baltimore stuck out because the houses looked alike because the steps, you know, in Baltimore, the steps are right on the sidewalk, and that's why I remember we did play Baltimore with -- you know, you have something to identify with when you're a kid, and it would be some things that maybe

an adult wouldn't identify with, but when you've been to all these different cities and all of a sudden you come upon a city and the steps are on the sidewalk, you know, you know that really looks odd to you.

But the minstrel shows, they would have like, maybe 10 or 12 acts, and they would put on a 2 or 3 hour show, with intermission. And they used to sell the programs and they would sell photographs, that's really the thing you do -- you sell your act -- would try to sell your photographs. And you sell them coming in the show; now you wouldn't sell too many when the show would start, but at the end of the show, the acts that they really loved, they really would buy the photographs.
You know, in later years after I was with Nat, we played -- who's the woman who did "Some of These Days"? Sophie Tucker?
Sophie Tucker was on the beach with us in Miami -- that was about in 1956 maybe, and she was selling her book after the show. So show business doesn't really change that much, you know?
She'd never sold her books before the show, and so I was telling the guys that that's what we used to do when I was a kid, and she was sitting right out there, but
they loved her show, see, and now they were gonna buy it, you know.
